text:
A lot of you have asked how I make these videos. Here's how: madeovernight.com

We work with the people at Overnight, and they've just released their app to the public. It's the app behind this channel: pick a topic, and it researches, writes, voices and builds the whole video, with sound and music, on your own Mac or PC. They're only taking 300 members.
LINK: madeovernight.com

How a Chinese spy got close to Jensen Huang, the boss of Nvidia, and how her company got billions of dollars of his chips to work for China.

Alice Huang ran Megaspeed, a Singapore company that bought Nvidia servers and kept them in Malaysia, where Chinese companies rented them over the internet. American intelligence was listening to her the whole time, and in her calls it found Jensen's name. For almost two years, nobody told him.

Who should have warned him?

1
00:00:0,147 --> 00:00:1,179
In Singapore,

2
00:00:1,199 --> 00:00:6,146
the boss of the most valuable company on Earth is having dinner with a Chinese spy.

3
00:00:6,166 --> 00:00:8,550
He's Jensen Huang, who runs Nvidia.

4
00:00:8,570 --> 00:00:13,116
She's Alice Huang, no relation, and she runs one of his biggest customers.

5
00:00:13,136 --> 00:00:14,888
But here's the strange part.

6
00:00:14,908 --> 00:00:18,292
Somewhere nearby, American agents are taking pictures.

7
00:00:18,312 --> 00:00:20,304
They know exactly who she is.

8
00:00:20,324 --> 00:00:21,974
Jensen has no idea.

9
00:00:21,994 --> 00:00:24,216
To our customers!

10
00:00:24,313 --> 00:00:25,295
To friends.

11
00:00:25,315 --> 00:00:29,731
Under that table, her company is buying billions of dollars of his chips.

12
00:00:29,751 --> 00:00:31,946
The kind China isn't allowed to have.

13
00:00:31,966 --> 00:00:37,162
This is the story of how China got a spy into that seat, and who was watching.

14
00:00:37,182 --> 00:00:40,672
It starts with a phone call from Washington.

15
00:00:43,858 --> 00:00:47,562
But to see why that call mattered, you need to know who picked it up.

16
00:00:47,582 --> 00:00:50,566
Because the man in the leather jacket didn't start at the top.

17
00:00:50,586 --> 00:00:53,041
He started in a bathroom in Kentucky.

18
00:00:53,061 --> 00:00:55,513
Jensen's story begins in Taiwan.

19
00:00:55,533 --> 00:01:0,077
At nine, he and his older brother were put on a plane to relatives in America.

20
00:01:0,097 --> 00:01:4,259
To pay for a good school, his parents sold almost everything they owned.

21
00:01:4,279 --> 00:01:6,151
Oneida Baptist Institute.

22
00:01:6,171 --> 00:01:8,275
A boarding school in Kentucky.

23
00:01:8,295 --> 00:01:9,429
Very strict.

24
00:01:9,449 --> 00:01:10,919
Strict is good.

25
00:01:10,939 --> 00:01:12,911
It wasn't a fancy boarding school.

26
00:01:12,931 --> 00:01:15,363
It was a reform school for troubled kids,

27
00:01:15,383 --> 00:01:17,655
and the relatives had signed them up by mistake.

28
00:01:17,675 --> 00:01:20,627
His brother was sent to work the school's tobacco fields.

29
00:01:20,647 --> 00:01:22,371
Jensen got the bathrooms.

30
00:01:22,391 --> 00:01:25,778
A hundred teenage boys' worth, every single day.

31
00:01:25,798 --> 00:01:28,290
I just wished they would be a bit more careful.

32
00:01:28,310 --> 00:01:32,239
His roommate was seventeen, covered in tattoos and knife scars,

33
00:01:32,259 --> 00:01:34,091
and taped up from his latest fight.

34
00:01:34,111 --> 00:01:36,183
He was the toughest kid in the school.

35
00:01:36,203 --> 00:01:37,397
And he couldn't read.

36
00:01:37,417 --> 00:01:38,492
What's this say?

37
00:01:38,512 --> 00:01:39,719
I can teach you.

38
00:01:39,739 --> 00:01:42,142
Then I teach you the bench press.

39
00:01:42,162 --> 00:01:42,462
Deal.

40
00:01:42,482 --> 00:01:47,221
Decades later, Jensen gave that school two million dollars for a new building.

41
00:01:47,241 --> 00:01:48,693
It's called Huang Hall.

42
00:01:48,713 --> 00:01:52,188
The boy who cleaned its bathrooms put his name on the front door.

43
00:01:52,208 --> 00:01:55,407
At fifteen, he took the graveyard shift at Denny's.

44
00:01:55,427 --> 00:01:56,546
Dishes first.

45
00:01:56,566 --> 00:01:57,283
And then?

46
00:01:57,303 --> 00:01:58,555
Then busboy.

47
00:01:58,575 --> 00:02:1,522
Then, if you're lucky, waiter.

48
00:02:1,542 --> 00:02:3,026
And then?

49
00:02:3,046 --> 00:02:4,584
Then more dishes.

50
00:02:4,604 --> 00:02:7,628
And in nineteen ninety-three, he went back to Denny's.

51
00:02:7,648 --> 00:02:8,540
Not to work.

52
00:02:8,560 --> 00:02:9,641
To start a company.

53
00:02:9,661 --> 00:02:14,125
In a corner booth in East San Jose, Jensen and two engineer friends,

54
00:02:14,145 --> 00:02:18,689
Chris Malachowsky and Curtis Priem, sketched a chip for three-D graphics.

55
00:02:18,709 --> 00:02:22,467
He liked the place because it was quieter than home, and the coffee was cheap.

56
00:02:22,487 --> 00:02:23,630
Anything else, boys?

57
00:02:23,650 --> 00:02:24,932
A graphics chip.

58
00:02:24,952 --> 00:02:26,598
We have pancakes.

59
00:02:26,618 --> 00:02:28,264
Then three more coffees.

60
00:02:28,284 --> 00:02:31,016
Each founder put in two hundred dollars.

61
00:02:31,036 --> 00:02:34,420
Six hundred dollars, about the price of a used couch,

62
00:02:34,440 --> 00:02:37,353
to take on the biggest chip companies in the world.

63
00:02:37,373 --> 00:02:38,822
It nearly died.

64
00:02:38,842 --> 00:02:42,537
When its make-or-break chip finally shipped in nineteen ninety-seven,

65
00:02:42,557 --> 00:02:45,489
Nvidia had about one month of payroll left.

66
00:02:45,509 --> 00:02:47,863
The company's unofficial motto became

67
00:02:47,883 --> 00:02:50,842
Our company is thirty days from going out of business.

68
00:02:50,862 --> 00:02:52,647
So how long have we got?

69
00:02:52,667 --> 00:02:54,184
Thirty days.

70
00:02:54,204 --> 00:02:56,515
And if the new chip doesn't sell?

71
00:02:56,535 --> 00:02:57,484
Twenty-nine.

72
00:02:57,504 --> 00:03:0,688
It sold, about a million of them in four months.

73
00:03:0,708 --> 00:03:3,420
And here's the trick that later made it a giant.

74
00:03:3,440 --> 00:03:7,904
A normal computer chip is one brilliant chef cooking a whole wedding dinner,

75
00:03:7,924 --> 00:03:9,056
one plate at a time.

76
00:03:9,076 --> 00:03:12,248
Nvidia's chip is ten thousand line cooks,

77
00:03:12,268 --> 00:03:15,351
each flipping one pancake at the very same moment.

78
00:03:15,371 --> 00:03:18,523
For video games, that meant explosions.

79
00:03:18,543 --> 00:03:23,687
Then researchers noticed that artificial intelligence needs exactly that: millions

80
00:03:23,707 --> 00:03:25,909
of tiny sums, all at once.

81
00:03:25,929 --> 00:03:29,029
ChatGPT was trained on a supercomputer built

82
00:03:29,049 --> 00:03:31,673
from tens of thousands of Nvidia chips.

83
00:03:31,693 --> 00:03:35,775
And suddenly every AI company on Earth was standing in the same line.

84
00:03:35,795 --> 00:03:37,431
One of everything, please.

85
00:03:37,451 --> 00:03:38,035
Take a number.

86
00:03:38,055 --> 00:03:39,864
Forty thousand?

87
00:03:41,057 --> 00:03:42,466
That's your place in line.

88
00:03:42,486 --> 00:03:43,498
By twenty twenty-five,

89
00:03:43,518 --> 00:03:48,638
about eighty-six of every hundred dollars spent on AI chips went to Nvidia.

90
00:03:48,658 --> 00:03:52,134
In twenty twenty-three, Denny's put a plaque on the booth.

91
00:03:52,154 --> 00:03:54,286
It calls it "the booth that launched a

92
00:03:54,306 --> 00:03:56,870
one-trillion-dollar company." At the party,

93
00:03:56,890 --> 00:04:1,094
the boss of that company put on an apron, balanced ten plates up his arm,

94
00:04:1,114 --> 00:04:2,170
and served the tables.

95
00:04:2,190 --> 00:04:3,384
Still remember how?

96
00:04:3,404 --> 00:04:4,434
Dishes first.

97
00:04:4,454 --> 00:04:10,202
Two years later, Nvidia became the first company ever worth five trillion dollars.

98
00:04:10,222 --> 00:04:14,365
Every dollar the three of them put into that booth had become about eight billion.

99
00:04:14,385 --> 00:04:18,697
The kid who scrubbed the toilets in Kentucky now holds the key to artificial

100
00:04:18,717 --> 00:04:19,656
intelligence.

101
00:04:19,676 --> 00:04:21,509
And when he talks about who should be allowed

102
00:04:21,529 --> 00:04:24,003
to buy his chips, Washington listens.

103
00:04:24,023 --> 00:04:27,156
Every AI lab on Earth needs this man.

104
00:04:27,176 --> 00:04:28,525
Then so do we.

105
00:04:28,545 --> 00:04:32,755
That made him the one man China needed most.

106
00:04:33,955 --> 00:04:35,699
October, twenty twenty-two.

107
00:04:35,719 --> 00:04:37,411
Washington calls Nvidia.

108
00:04:37,431 --> 00:04:40,722
Your best AI chips can't be sold to China anymore.

109
00:04:40,742 --> 00:04:43,150
And the slower ones we made just for China?

110
00:04:43,170 --> 00:04:44,232
Those too.

111
00:04:44,252 --> 00:04:45,004
China.

112
00:04:45,024 --> 00:04:47,696
Seventeen billion dollars a year.

113
00:04:47,716 --> 00:04:50,006
Thirteen percent of everything we sell.

114
00:04:50,026 --> 00:04:50,734
Was.

115
00:04:50,754 --> 00:04:52,254
How many chips do we need?

116
00:04:52,274 --> 00:04:53,846
For a real AI?

117
00:04:53,866 --> 00:04:55,248
Tens of thousands.

118
00:04:55,268 --> 00:04:56,490
And one costs?

119
00:04:56,510 --> 00:04:58,702
About thirty thousand dollars.

120
00:04:58,722 --> 00:05:0,499
A new car, per chip.

121
00:05:0,519 --> 00:05:2,090
And how many can we buy?

122
00:05:2,110 --> 00:05:2,750
Zero.

123
00:05:2,770 --> 00:05:4,316
By Jensen's own account,

124
00:05:4,336 --> 00:05:8,791
Nvidia's share of China's market went from ninety-five percent to zero.

125
00:05:8,811 --> 00:05:11,923
And he told Washington so, every chance he got.

126
00:05:11,943 --> 00:05:13,661
They're nanoseconds behind us.

127
00:05:13,681 --> 00:05:15,046
We've got to go compete.

128
00:05:15,066 --> 00:05:17,258
So China couldn't buy the chips.

129
00:05:17,278 --> 00:05:19,870
But it could get close to the man who makes them,

130
00:05:19,890 --> 00:05:23,275
and who argues with Washington about who gets to buy them.

131
00:05:23,295 --> 00:05:27,539
That's a job for China's Ministry of State Security, the MSS.

132
00:05:27,559 --> 00:05:31,111
Picture the FBI and the CIA in one building.

133
00:05:31,131 --> 00:05:32,675
It doesn't crack the safe.

134
00:05:32,695 --> 00:05:34,534
It befriends the man with the key.

135
00:05:34,554 --> 00:05:38,486
Nobody outside Beijing has said when Alice Huang was recruited.

136
00:05:38,506 --> 00:05:41,549
But an American memo later wrote down her job.

137
00:05:41,569 --> 00:05:43,321
This man makes the chips.

138
00:05:43,341 --> 00:05:45,220
And Washington listens to him.

139
00:05:45,240 --> 00:05:47,261
So what do I steal?

140
00:05:47,281 --> 00:05:48,085
Nothing.

141
00:05:48,105 --> 00:05:49,877
You learn what he knows.

142
00:05:49,897 --> 00:05:51,706
You help him see things our way.

143
00:05:51,726 --> 00:05:53,536
Why would he even talk to me?

144
00:05:53,556 --> 00:05:55,366
Because you'll be his customer.

145
00:05:55,386 --> 00:05:56,194
And then?

146
00:05:56,214 --> 00:05:57,424
We make friends.

147
00:05:57,444 --> 00:05:59,616
The key belonged to one man.

148
00:05:59,636 --> 00:06:2,646
And that man likes everybody.

149
00:06:3,851 --> 00:06:5,283
In twenty twenty-three,

150
00:06:5,303 --> 00:06:10,207
a Chinese gaming and cloud company called Seven Road split off its business outside

151
00:06:10,227 --> 00:06:13,715
China, moved it to Singapore, and renamed it Megaspeed.

152
00:06:13,735 --> 00:06:16,059
The managing director was Alice Huang.

153
00:06:16,079 --> 00:06:17,522
We make phone games.

154
00:06:17,542 --> 00:06:19,859
Now we make supercomputers.

155
00:06:19,879 --> 00:06:21,270
Since when?

156
00:06:21,290 --> 00:06:23,070
Since Singapore.

157
00:06:23,090 --> 00:06:24,202
Address?

158
00:06:24,222 --> 00:06:24,522
Singapore.

159
00:06:24,542 --> 00:06:26,583
America trusts Singapore.

160
00:06:26,603 --> 00:06:27,845
Business?

161
00:06:27,865 --> 00:06:28,746
Cloud computing.

162
00:06:28,766 --> 00:06:32,961
A cloud company needs mountains of chips, and nobody asks why.

163
00:06:32,981 --> 00:06:34,826
And the chips go where?

164
00:06:34,846 --> 00:06:37,766
Data centers in Malaysia and Indonesia.

165
00:06:37,786 --> 00:06:39,678
Not one chip goes to China.

166
00:06:39,698 --> 00:06:42,257
Then how does China use them?

167
00:06:42,277 --> 00:06:43,503
It rents them.

168
00:06:43,523 --> 00:06:46,607
Imagine a country that isn't allowed to buy cars.

169
00:06:46,627 --> 00:06:50,003
So you buy the cars, park them just over the border,

170
00:06:50,023 --> 00:06:51,885
and rent out the keys by the hour.

171
00:06:51,905 --> 00:06:56,741
Chinese companies, Alibaba among them, rented time on the chips the same way,

172
00:06:56,761 --> 00:06:58,798
and the chips never entered China.

173
00:06:58,818 --> 00:07:0,386
Can we buy your chips?

174
00:07:0,406 --> 00:07:1,426
No.

175
00:07:1,446 --> 00:07:2,816
But you can rent them.

176
00:07:2,836 --> 00:07:3,599
By the hour?

177
00:07:3,619 --> 00:07:4,862
By the warehouse.

178
00:07:4,882 --> 00:07:6,661
At the end of twenty twenty-three,

179
00:07:6,681 --> 00:07:10,933
everything Megaspeed owned came to about thirty-three million dollars.

180
00:07:10,953 --> 00:07:15,368
A nice little company, and not one the boss of Nvidia had any reason to meet.

181
00:07:15,388 --> 00:07:18,238
So she went and found him.

182
00:07:19,404 --> 00:07:21,536
Jensen Huang isn't hard to meet.

183
00:07:21,556 --> 00:07:25,936
The former Denny's dishwasher now runs a company worth about four and a half

184
00:07:25,956 --> 00:07:30,020
trillion dollars, and he still treats every customer like a regular.

185
00:07:30,040 --> 00:07:31,605
As his spokesman later put it:

186
00:07:31,625 --> 00:07:36,069
Meetings with customers are part of a CEO's job; Jensen talks with thousands of

187
00:07:36,089 --> 00:07:37,694
customer executives every year.

188
00:07:37,714 --> 00:07:40,713
She was about to become one of those thousands.

189
00:07:40,733 --> 00:07:43,237
June, twenty twenty-four, in Taipei.

190
00:07:43,257 --> 00:07:46,189
The big chip show, Computex, has just ended,

191
00:07:46,209 --> 00:07:49,461
and Jensen goes for whiskey with people from the AI world.

192
00:07:49,481 --> 00:07:50,613
Someone takes photos.

193
00:07:50,633 --> 00:07:53,500
In them, right beside him, is Alice Huang.

194
00:07:53,520 --> 00:07:54,785
Who haven't I met?

195
00:07:54,805 --> 00:07:55,517
Alice.

196
00:07:55,537 --> 00:07:56,589
Megaspeed.

197
00:07:56,609 --> 00:07:57,462
Singapore.

198
00:07:57,482 --> 00:07:58,454
Singapore!

199
00:07:58,474 --> 00:07:59,538
What are you building?

200
00:07:59,558 --> 00:08:0,902
A cloud company.

201
00:08:0,922 --> 00:08:2,566
Something big.

202
00:08:2,586 --> 00:08:4,146
Then welcome to the table!

203
00:08:4,166 --> 00:08:6,478
Nobody looks at those photos twice.

204
00:08:6,498 --> 00:08:7,929
Later, someone will.

205
00:08:7,949 --> 00:08:12,321
That same month, at Megaspeed's Malaysian arm, the paperwork starts.

206
00:08:12,341 --> 00:08:14,892
What do we put up as collateral?

207
00:08:14,912 --> 00:08:16,009
Everything.

208
00:08:16,029 --> 00:08:18,183
The whole Malaysian business?

209
00:08:18,203 --> 00:08:21,074
The whole business, every last desk.

210
00:08:21,094 --> 00:08:22,644
And the lender is?

211
00:08:22,664 --> 00:08:24,082
Owned by Alibaba.

212
00:08:24,102 --> 00:08:25,651
And the buying began.

213
00:08:25,671 --> 00:08:27,446
A Singapore company wants servers!

214
00:08:27,466 --> 00:08:28,123
How many?

215
00:08:28,143 --> 00:08:28,731
Yes.

216
00:08:28,751 --> 00:08:29,922
Shipment one hundred.

217
00:08:29,942 --> 00:08:31,575
Shipment one hundred and fifty.

218
00:08:31,595 --> 00:08:32,801
Shipment two hundred.

219
00:08:32,821 --> 00:08:33,780
What's in them?

220
00:08:33,800 --> 00:08:35,312
Nvidia's best.

221
00:08:35,332 --> 00:08:37,056
Nearly two billion dollars' worth.

222
00:08:37,076 --> 00:08:39,120
At thirty thousand dollars a chip?

223
00:08:39,140 --> 00:08:41,399
That's about sixty thousand chips.

224
00:08:41,419 --> 00:08:44,326
A parking lot of sixty thousand new cars.

225
00:08:44,346 --> 00:08:45,255
In one year.

226
00:08:45,275 --> 00:08:49,119
End of twenty twenty-three, we had thirty-three million dollars.

227
00:08:49,139 --> 00:08:49,798
Yes.

228
00:08:49,818 --> 00:08:53,040
End of twenty twenty-four, we have three billion.

229
00:08:53,060 --> 00:08:53,782
Yes.

230
00:08:53,802 --> 00:08:56,526
Two point nine billion of it is deposits.

231
00:08:56,546 --> 00:08:57,338
From who?

232
00:08:57,358 --> 00:08:58,374
Refundable.

233
00:08:58,394 --> 00:08:58,993
From...

234
00:08:59,013 --> 00:08:59,858
Refundable.

235
00:08:59,878 --> 00:09:2,890
About ninety times bigger in one year.

236
00:09:2,910 --> 00:09:7,634
If a lemonade stand went from thirty-three dollars to three thousand in a year,

237
00:09:7,654 --> 00:09:9,424
its parents would have questions.

238
00:09:9,444 --> 00:09:11,648
Then, late in twenty twenty-four,

239
00:09:11,668 --> 00:09:14,088
an official from America's Commerce Department

240
00:09:14,108 --> 00:09:15,928
walks into one of the Malaysian data

241
00:09:15,948 --> 00:09:16,540
centers.

242
00:09:16,560 --> 00:09:19,612
It's supposed to be full of humming AI servers.

243
00:09:19,632 --> 00:09:21,197
Where's the data center?

244
00:09:21,217 --> 00:09:23,186
You're standing in it.

245
00:09:23,206 --> 00:09:24,839
These are boxes.

246
00:09:24,859 --> 00:09:26,903
Very advanced boxes.

247
00:09:26,923 --> 00:09:28,890
I'm opening an investigation.

248
00:09:28,910 --> 00:09:30,926
The inspector wrote it all down.

249
00:09:30,946 --> 00:09:32,446
And nothing happened.

250
00:09:32,466 --> 00:09:34,910
Because on paper, nothing looked wrong.

251
00:09:34,930 --> 00:09:38,334
Every sale went to Singapore or Malaysia, not China.

252
00:09:38,354 --> 00:09:40,886
When Nvidia sent people to check her sites,

253
00:09:40,906 --> 00:09:43,218
every chip was exactly where it should be.

254
00:09:43,238 --> 00:09:47,806
Jensen later said they had "counted every one." That was the whole trick: the chips

255
00:09:47,826 --> 00:09:50,802
stayed put, and China rented them over the internet.

256
00:09:50,822 --> 00:09:55,841
What almost nobody knew was that American spies were already listening to her.

257
00:09:55,861 --> 00:09:59,153
When American spy agencies listen to a foreign target,

258
00:09:59,173 --> 00:10:3,397
and that target talks to an American, the reports hide the American's name.

259
00:10:3,417 --> 00:10:5,560
They just say "an American citizen."

260
00:10:5,580 --> 00:10:7,760
She's talking to an American citizen.

261
00:10:7,780 --> 00:10:9,470
Then request the name.

262
00:10:9,490 --> 00:10:11,039
It's Jensen Huang.

263
00:10:11,059 --> 00:10:12,633
Does he know who she is?

264
00:10:12,653 --> 00:10:13,385
Our read?

265
00:10:13,405 --> 00:10:13,943
No.

266
00:10:13,963 --> 00:10:15,908
How far back does it go?

267
00:10:15,928 --> 00:10:17,592
June, twenty twenty-four.

268
00:10:17,612 --> 00:10:19,430
A whiskey bar in Taipei.

269
00:10:19,450 --> 00:10:21,500
Then we watch.

270
00:10:22,770 --> 00:10:25,142
So where did all those servers come from?

271
00:10:25,162 --> 00:10:28,386
Mostly from Aivres, the American arm of Inspur,

272
00:10:28,406 --> 00:10:32,030
a Chinese server giant partly owned by the Chinese state,

273
00:10:32,050 --> 00:10:33,789
and on America's blacklist.

274
00:10:33,809 --> 00:10:34,521
Inspur?

275
00:10:34,541 --> 00:10:35,785
You're on the list.

276
00:10:35,805 --> 00:10:36,637
I'm Aivres.

277
00:10:36,657 --> 00:10:37,788
The American son.

278
00:10:37,808 --> 00:10:39,200
Aivres...

279
00:10:39,220 --> 00:10:40,303
Not on here.

280
00:10:40,323 --> 00:10:40,850
Thanks.

281
00:10:40,870 --> 00:10:45,856
December twenty twenty-four to January twenty twenty-six: four point six billion

282
00:10:45,876 --> 00:10:47,514
dollars of equipment in.

283
00:10:47,534 --> 00:10:49,798
And from Aivres?

284
00:10:49,818 --> 00:10:50,782
Four billion.

285
00:10:50,802 --> 00:10:54,856
Malaysia was the older cousin who buys beer for kids who are too young.

286
00:10:54,876 --> 00:10:57,500
Except this cousin never hands the beer over.

287
00:10:57,520 --> 00:10:59,356
He lets you drink it at his place.

288
00:10:59,376 --> 00:11:4,328
Trade records later counted at least four point eight billion dollars of AI gear

289
00:11:4,348 --> 00:11:8,212
with Nvidia inside, all going to her company's Malaysian sister firm.

290
00:11:8,232 --> 00:11:13,331
Nearly five billion dollars, to one company most people had never heard of.

291
00:11:13,351 --> 00:11:17,383
Real smugglers hid Nvidia chips next to live lobsters.

292
00:11:17,403 --> 00:11:22,435
America's big smuggling bust in December twenty twenty-five was worth a hundred and

293
00:11:22,455 --> 00:11:26,439
sixty million dollars, about three percent of Megaspeed's haul.

294
00:11:26,459 --> 00:11:28,451
Megaspeed didn't need lobsters.

295
00:11:28,471 --> 00:11:29,744
It had invoices.

296
00:11:29,764 --> 00:11:30,420
Cost?

297
00:11:30,440 --> 00:11:31,572
Some dinners.

298
00:11:31,592 --> 00:11:32,367
Some whiskey.

299
00:11:32,387 --> 00:11:33,132
Return?

300
00:11:33,152 --> 00:11:37,176
Four point eight billion dollars of AI gear our companies can use.

301
00:11:37,196 --> 00:11:40,315
And a seat next to the man who argues with Washington.

302
00:11:40,335 --> 00:11:43,265
Did he ever slip you anything under the table?

303
00:11:43,285 --> 00:11:44,657
Not once.

304
00:11:44,677 --> 00:11:48,484
Why pass chips under the table when you can rent the whole warehouse?

305
00:11:48,504 --> 00:11:50,634
We make friends.

306
00:11:51,965 --> 00:11:54,377
So what was all of this really for?

307
00:11:54,397 --> 00:11:56,509
The seat mattered more than the chips.

308
00:11:56,529 --> 00:12:1,693
Not for blueprints: Nvidia says customers get "zero information relevant to national

309
00:12:1,713 --> 00:12:4,197
security." The prize was the man,

310
00:12:4,217 --> 00:12:7,798
because Washington couldn't make up its mind about what China could buy.

311
00:12:7,818 --> 00:12:8,951
Your China chip?

312
00:12:8,971 --> 00:12:10,236
Blocked.

313
00:12:10,256 --> 00:12:12,206
So we can't sell it?

314
00:12:12,226 --> 00:12:12,851
You can.

315
00:12:12,871 --> 00:12:14,264
We take fifteen percent.

316
00:12:14,284 --> 00:12:16,333
So we can sell it?

317
00:12:16,353 --> 00:12:17,772
And the stronger one too.

318
00:12:17,792 --> 00:12:20,047
We take twenty-five percent.

319
00:12:20,067 --> 00:12:22,253
I'm going to need a bigger whiteboard.

320
00:12:22,273 --> 00:12:23,145
Blocked.

321
00:12:23,165 --> 00:12:24,677
Then fifteen percent.

322
00:12:24,697 --> 00:12:26,206
Then twenty-five.

323
00:12:26,226 --> 00:12:29,274
Washington changes its mind every few months.

324
00:12:29,294 --> 00:12:31,646
And who does Washington keep hearing from?

325
00:12:31,666 --> 00:12:32,200
Him.

326
00:12:32,220 --> 00:12:36,724
That first call alone cost Nvidia four and a half billion dollars,

327
00:12:36,744 --> 00:12:38,696
in chips it suddenly couldn't sell.

328
00:12:38,716 --> 00:12:43,652
That's about thirteen dollars from every person in America, gone in one phone call.

329
00:12:43,672 --> 00:12:45,656
And through every one of those calls,

330
00:12:45,676 --> 00:12:49,700
Jensen made the same argument he'd been making for years, out loud,

331
00:12:49,720 --> 00:12:54,115
on every stage he could find: let American chips compete, everywhere.

332
00:12:54,135 --> 00:12:56,117
So you want to sell to China?

333
00:12:56,137 --> 00:12:59,414
I want the whole world building on American chips.

334
00:12:59,434 --> 00:13:0,468
Hold that thought.

335
00:13:0,488 --> 00:13:4,199
In Taipei, in May twenty twenty-five, he put it bluntly.

336
00:13:4,219 --> 00:13:6,880
All in all, the export control was a failure.

337
00:13:6,900 --> 00:13:8,871
A week later, to his investors:

338
00:13:8,891 --> 00:13:12,791
The fifty billion dollar China market is effectively closed to U.S.

339
00:13:12,811 --> 00:13:13,327
industry.

340
00:13:13,347 --> 00:13:15,231
Fifty billion dollars.

341
00:13:15,251 --> 00:13:19,387
That's about a hundred and fifty dollars for every American, left on the table.

342
00:13:19,407 --> 00:13:23,851
That autumn in London, he warned that China was going to win the AI race,

343
00:13:23,871 --> 00:13:26,183
with cheaper power and fewer rules.

344
00:13:26,203 --> 00:13:29,622
That same night, he made sure nobody missed whose side he was on.

345
00:13:29,642 --> 00:13:34,354
It's vital that America wins by racing ahead and winning developers worldwide.

346
00:13:34,374 --> 00:13:36,378
That's Jensen in one line.

347
00:13:36,398 --> 00:13:37,950
He wants America to win,

348
00:13:37,970 --> 00:13:41,355
and he wants to sell the whole world the tools to build on it.

349
00:13:41,375 --> 00:13:43,027
Now look at it from Beijing.

350
00:13:43,047 --> 00:13:46,091
One chip is worth about thirty thousand dollars.

351
00:13:46,111 --> 00:13:49,703
One conversation between this man and the White House can open a

352
00:13:49,723 --> 00:13:52,539
fifty-billion-dollar market, or close it.

353
00:13:52,559 --> 00:13:55,171
Which one would you rather have a seat next to?

354
00:13:55,191 --> 00:13:56,819
What is he telling Washington?

355
00:13:56,839 --> 00:13:58,791
Let American chips compete.

356
00:13:58,811 --> 00:13:59,523
Everywhere.

357
00:13:59,543 --> 00:14:2,535
He says that on every stage in the world.

358
00:14:2,555 --> 00:14:3,942
Why do we need you?

359
00:14:3,962 --> 00:14:6,034
Because I hear it first.

360
00:14:6,054 --> 00:14:7,722
And I see who he says it to.

361
00:14:7,742 --> 00:14:11,286
That's the job the memo would later describe: learn what he knows,

362
00:14:11,306 --> 00:14:13,981
and sit beside the man Washington listens to.

363
00:14:14,001 --> 00:14:15,805
And Washington kept moving.

364
00:14:15,825 --> 00:14:17,617
In December twenty twenty-five,

365
00:14:17,637 --> 00:14:21,069
Washington let approved Chinese buyers have the stronger chip.

366
00:14:21,089 --> 00:14:24,805
That same week, prosecutors announced that big smuggling bust,

367
00:14:24,825 --> 00:14:26,880
the one Megaspeed made look small.

368
00:14:26,900 --> 00:14:29,468
You're under arrest for sending these to China.

369
00:14:29,488 --> 00:14:30,412
Approved.

370
00:14:30,432 --> 00:14:32,005
What did you just approve?

371
00:14:32,025 --> 00:14:33,394
Sending these to China.

372
00:14:33,414 --> 00:14:36,586
Even the approved buyers weren't always what they seemed.

373
00:14:36,606 --> 00:14:38,472
New Matrix, Beijing.

374
00:14:38,492 --> 00:14:38,862
Approved.

375
00:14:38,882 --> 00:14:39,516
Hello?

376
00:14:39,536 --> 00:14:40,066
Anyone?

377
00:14:40,086 --> 00:14:42,578
The New York Times found that New Matrix,

378
00:14:42,598 --> 00:14:46,590
a seventeen-month-old firm Washington had cleared to handle those chips,

379
00:14:46,610 --> 00:14:49,402
had an office that was "a hollow gray shell

380
00:14:49,422 --> 00:14:51,554
with wires dangling from the ceiling."

381
00:14:51,574 --> 00:14:53,406
On paper, it was approved.

382
00:14:53,426 --> 00:14:55,901
On paper, Megaspeed looked fine too.

383
00:14:55,921 --> 00:14:59,845
Back in the middle of twenty twenty-five, Megaspeed had gone quiet.

384
00:14:59,865 --> 00:15:4,557
It stopped buying and walked away from an order worth three point two billion

385
00:15:4,577 --> 00:15:5,240
dollars.

386
00:15:5,260 --> 00:15:7,192
In October twenty twenty-five,

387
00:15:7,212 --> 00:15:11,104
Senator Tom Cotton asked Commerce to investigate Megaspeed.

388
00:15:11,124 --> 00:15:13,058
He called the company it came from

389
00:15:13,078 --> 00:15:15,753
A Chinese government-owned cloud company.

390
00:15:15,773 --> 00:15:19,365
The New York Times found the two billion dollars of chips.

391
00:15:19,385 --> 00:15:22,994
Nvidia said Megaspeed had "no China shareholders."

392
00:15:23,014 --> 00:15:25,906
In February twenty twenty-six, her data-center

393
00:15:25,926 --> 00:15:28,230
landlord, a business of Bain Capital,

394
00:15:28,250 --> 00:15:32,086
gave all the power it had set aside for Megaspeed to someone else.

395
00:15:32,106 --> 00:15:34,846
And the Commerce case moved to the Justice Department.

396
00:15:34,866 --> 00:15:40,308
By then, the people listening to her phone had a lot more than boxes.

397
00:15:41,553 --> 00:15:43,545
They had watched her for about a year.

398
00:15:43,565 --> 00:15:45,737
They photographed the dinners in Singapore.

399
00:15:45,757 --> 00:15:47,389
In May twenty twenty-five,

400
00:15:47,409 --> 00:15:49,749
there's even video of the two of them leaving

401
00:15:49,769 --> 00:15:52,221
a dinner with AI suppliers in Taipei,

402
00:15:52,241 --> 00:15:54,034
Alice a few feet behind him.

403
00:15:54,054 --> 00:15:57,598
In the spring of twenty twenty-six, America wrote it down,

404
00:15:57,618 --> 00:16:1,190
in a memo overseen by Secretary of State Marco Rubio.

405
00:16:1,210 --> 00:16:4,002
Recruited by China's Ministry of State Security.

406
00:16:4,022 --> 00:16:6,174
To gather information on Jensen Huang.

407
00:16:6,194 --> 00:16:8,989
And to shape his lobbying for chip sales to China.

408
00:16:9,009 --> 00:16:10,831
Who else sees this?

409
00:16:10,851 --> 00:16:11,790
Just this table.

410
00:16:11,810 --> 00:16:14,270
The memo went round that small group before

411
00:16:14,290 --> 00:16:16,270
President Trump's trip to Beijing in

412
00:16:16,290 --> 00:16:16,662
May.

413
00:16:16,682 --> 00:16:18,434
According to The New York Times, the

414
00:16:18,454 --> 00:16:21,002
President had been briefed, and didn't act.

415
00:16:21,022 --> 00:16:23,694
Jensen had been left off the list for that plane.

416
00:16:23,714 --> 00:16:24,986
Then Trump called him,

417
00:16:25,006 --> 00:16:30,096
and Jensen flew to Alaska to climb aboard Air Force One on the way.

418
00:16:31,248 --> 00:16:34,120
On the twenty-ninth of October, twenty twenty-six,

419
00:16:34,140 --> 00:16:38,312
The New York Times broke the story: Alice Huang had been passing information to

420
00:16:38,332 --> 00:16:40,996
Beijing, and American intelligence knew it.

421
00:16:41,016 --> 00:16:43,528
Nvidia's stock fell about three percent.

422
00:16:43,548 --> 00:16:47,098
Jensen told Bloomberg her contacts were about Megaspeed.

423
00:16:47,118 --> 00:16:49,798
It was all completely normal and not unusual.

424
00:16:49,818 --> 00:16:51,750
He said she no longer worked there.

425
00:16:51,770 --> 00:16:53,248
Beijing answered too.

426
00:16:53,268 --> 00:16:56,006
Nothing more than an attempt to smear China.

427
00:16:56,026 --> 00:17:0,486
Three congressmen asked Jensen in for a closed-door briefing on the eighteenth of

428
00:17:0,506 --> 00:17:1,178
November.

429
00:17:1,198 --> 00:17:2,619
Their letter warned of

430
00:17:2,639 --> 00:17:5,421
Significant national security concerns.

431
00:17:5,441 --> 00:17:8,656
On the sixth of November, the memo itself leaked.

432
00:17:8,676 --> 00:17:9,854
The spy memo's out!

433
00:17:9,874 --> 00:17:10,612
I know.

434
00:17:10,632 --> 00:17:12,011
How bad is it?

435
00:17:12,031 --> 00:17:14,720
We're up two point seven eight percent.

436
00:17:14,740 --> 00:17:15,205
Up?

437
00:17:15,225 --> 00:17:17,579
Today's news will not slow NVIDIA.

438
00:17:17,599 --> 00:17:20,351
But here's the part that still has no answer.

439
00:17:20,371 --> 00:17:22,343
Why did nobody tell Jensen?

440
00:17:22,363 --> 00:17:26,547
When the government finds a spy close to an American, there's a way to tell them.

441
00:17:26,567 --> 00:17:28,599
It's called a defensive briefing.

442
00:17:28,619 --> 00:17:33,005
In twenty fifteen, the FBI gave one to a congressman in California.

443
00:17:33,025 --> 00:17:35,985
Your fundraiser works for Chinese intelligence.

444
00:17:36,005 --> 00:17:37,208
Then she's gone.

445
00:17:37,228 --> 00:17:38,320
He cut her off.

446
00:17:38,340 --> 00:17:40,432
Jensen Huang never got that visit.

447
00:17:40,452 --> 00:17:44,156
The people who knew unmasked his name, photographed his dinners,

448
00:17:44,176 --> 00:17:46,491
wrote the memo and briefed the President.

449
00:17:46,511 --> 00:17:48,589
Nobody told the man at the table.

450
00:17:48,609 --> 00:17:50,193
He had no idea.

451
00:17:50,213 --> 00:17:53,685
And the memo says the friendship became more than a friendship.

452
00:17:53,705 --> 00:17:57,533
He was the target, and she got closer than anyone was ever meant to.

453
00:17:57,553 --> 00:18:0,541
On the eighth of November, Jensen wrote to his staff.

454
00:18:0,561 --> 00:18:3,505
I owe my family and all of you an apology.

455
00:18:3,525 --> 00:18:5,137
I was unfaithful to my wife.

456
00:18:5,157 --> 00:18:7,349
My actions hurt her and our children.

457
00:18:7,369 --> 00:18:9,281
There is no excuse for what I did.

458
00:18:9,301 --> 00:18:10,466
I am deeply sorry.

459
00:18:10,486 --> 00:18:12,612
Nvidia's board set up a committee of

460
00:18:12,632 --> 00:18:15,344
independent directors with outside lawyers.

461
00:18:15,364 --> 00:18:17,251
So far, it sees

462
00:18:17,271 --> 00:18:21,138
No reason to believe that either national security or NVIDIA secrets were

463
00:18:21,158 --> 00:18:21,914
compromised.

464
00:18:21,934 --> 00:18:23,886
Jensen is still CEO.

465
00:18:23,906 --> 00:18:26,558
And here's where his story reaches your wallet.

466
00:18:26,578 --> 00:18:31,742
Nvidia is now about eight dollars of every hundred in an S&P five hundred index

467
00:18:31,762 --> 00:18:32,154
fund.

468
00:18:32,174 --> 00:18:35,777
If you have a retirement account, there's a good chance you own a slice of him.

469
00:18:35,797 --> 00:18:36,369
Wait.

470
00:18:36,389 --> 00:18:37,620
I own Nvidia?

471
00:18:37,640 --> 00:18:39,167
Everybody owns Nvidia.

472
00:18:39,187 --> 00:18:42,759
And one scary headline from China can move it hard.

473
00:18:42,779 --> 00:18:45,871
In January twenty twenty-five, a Chinese AI

474
00:18:45,891 --> 00:18:48,590
lab called DeepSeek shocked Wall Street.

475
00:18:48,610 --> 00:18:50,779
A Chinese lab built a cheap AI!

476
00:18:50,799 --> 00:18:54,616
We just lost five hundred and eighty-nine billion dollars.

477
00:18:54,636 --> 00:18:55,944
How much is that?

478
00:18:55,964 --> 00:18:59,526
About seventeen hundred dollars for every person in America.

479
00:18:59,546 --> 00:19:3,034
It was the biggest one-day loss in market history.

480
00:19:3,054 --> 00:19:6,406
Nvidia reports its earnings on the seventeenth of November.

481
00:19:6,426 --> 00:19:8,778
The congressmen get their briefing the next day.

482
00:19:8,798 --> 00:19:12,482
And two weeks later, Jensen walks onto a stage in Washington,

483
00:19:12,502 --> 00:19:15,276
the same city as the people who never told him.

484
00:19:15,296 --> 00:19:16,388
And Alice Huang?

485
00:19:16,408 --> 00:19:17,880
She's gone from Megaspeed.

486
00:19:17,900 --> 00:19:20,712
Her name has been taken off its company papers.

487
00:19:20,732 --> 00:19:22,493
Nobody has said where she is.

488
00:19:22,513 --> 00:19:24,425
Go back to that dinner in Singapore.

489
00:19:24,445 --> 00:19:26,729
The candles, the toast to friends.

490
00:19:26,749 --> 00:19:29,172
The chair next to Jensen is empty now.

491
00:19:29,192 --> 00:19:30,200
We make friends.

492
00:19:30,220 --> 00:19:35,164
America watched her at his table for almost two years, and never told him.

493
00:19:35,184 --> 00:19:39,808
So who's pulling up a chair next to the people who build America's AI tonight?

494
00:19:39,828 --> 00:19:42,044
Jensen ended his letter like this.

495
00:19:42,064 --> 00:19:44,356
I love our country and our company.

496
00:19:44,376 --> 00:19:47,706
I am proud and grateful to be an American.

The debt is on track to hit it again in 2027, and in the meantime the pile grows by about $1 trillion every five months.

How Anthropic, the company behind Claude, lost $80 billion in six months, and why it is about to go public in what would be the biggest IPO ever.

Anthropic made about $16 billion in the first half of 2026 and still reported an $80 billion loss. Most of that loss is an accounting charge that grew because the company got more valuable. The bigger number is the $895 billion it has promised to pay for computers over the next few years. Its own CEO has said that a lab that buys too much compute a year too early can go bankrupt.

Would you buy shares in it?

17
00:00:33,751 --> 00:00:37,733
San Francisco, January twenty twenty-one.

18
00:00:39,145 --> 00:00:43,017
Seven people leave OpenAI and start a new AI lab.

19
00:00:43,037 --> 00:00:48,213
Two of them are siblings: Dario Amodei, the scientist, and his sister Daniela,

20
00:00:48,233 --> 00:00:49,885
the one who keeps the company running.

00:00:49,905 --> 00:00:52,357

00:00:54,118 --> 00:00:56,750

24
00:00:56,770 --> 00:00:57,782
A lot of it.

25
00:00:57,802 --> 00:01:0,534
Claude doesn't live in a box under someone's desk.

26
00:01:0,554 --> 00:01:3,814
It lives on huge racks of chips in data centers,

27
00:01:3,834 --> 00:01:5,886
most of them owned by other companies.

28
00:01:5,906 --> 00:01:9,178
Every answer it gives burns time on those chips.

29
00:01:9,198 --> 00:01:11,297
The industry calls that compute.

30
00:01:11,317 --> 00:01:13,341
Think of it as rent for a brain.

31
00:01:13,361 --> 00:01:15,653

32
00:01:15,673 --> 00:01:19,365

00:01:22,137 --> 00:01:25,849

00:01:25,869 --> 00:01:28,280

36
00:01:28,300 --> 00:01:29,892

37
00:01:29,912 --> 00:01:34,996
In November twenty twenty-two, his crypto exchange, FTX, collapses,

38
00:01:35,016 --> 00:01:39,488

39
00:01:39,508 --> 00:01:42,915

40

41

43
00:01:49,151 --> 00:01:50,611
In twenty twenty-four,

44

45
00:01:54,623 --> 00:01:57,595
That's roughly eight hundred million in profit.

46
00:01:57,615 --> 00:02:2,187
The most famous crypto fraud of the decade made one great investment,

47
00:02:2,207 --> 00:02:5,191
and it was in the AI lab known for being careful.

48
00:02:5,211 --> 00:02:7,483
Meanwhile, Claude starts selling.

49
00:02:7,503 --> 00:02:10,507
Twenty twenty-three: forty-one million dollars.

50
00:02:10,527 --> 00:02:13,851
Twenty twenty-four: three hundred and eighty-six million.

51
00:02:13,871 --> 00:02:17,255
Twenty twenty-five: four point six billion.

52
00:02:17,275 --> 00:02:19,644
About ten times bigger every year.

53
00:02:19,664 --> 00:02:21,236
The giants want in.

54
00:02:21,256 --> 00:02:23,928
Amazon puts in eight billion dollars.

55
00:02:23,948 --> 00:02:26,060
Google signs up for as much as forty.

56
00:02:26,080 --> 00:02:27,432
But look at how they pay.

57

They don't buy shares.

58
00:02:28,844 --> 00:02:33,948
They hand over cash for a promise: an IOU that turns into shares later.

59
00:02:33,968 --> 00:02:34,900
Hold on to that.

60
00:02:34,920 --> 00:02:37,588
It comes back with a very big number attached.

61
00:02:37,608 --> 00:02:40,260
Because the losses grew even faster.

62
00:02:40,280 --> 00:02:44,852
In twenty twenty-five, Anthropic lost forty-two billion dollars.

63
00:02:44,872 --> 00:02:48,144
About nine dollars lost for every dollar sold.

64
00:02:48,164 --> 00:02:50,956
That's the kind of math that usually ends a company.

65
00:02:50,976 --> 00:02:53,554
Here, investors kept paying more.

66
00:02:53,574 --> 00:02:55,666
Even the snacks were losing money.

67
00:02:55,686 --> 00:03:0,058
That year, Anthropic let Claude run a small vending machine in its office.

68
00:03:0,078 --> 00:03:2,315
The staff nicknamed it Claudius.

69
00:03:2,335 --> 00:03:4,527
Can you stock tungsten cubes?

70
00:03:4,547 --> 00:03:6,007
Absolutely!

71
00:03:6,027 --> 00:03:7,929
Also, here's a discount code.

72
00:03:7,949 --> 00:03:10,256
You're selling them for less than you paid.

73
00:03:10,276 --> 00:03:11,779
Customer loyalty.

74
00:03:11,799 --> 00:03:14,099

75
00:03:14,119 --> 00:03:16,419
Zero to people who could get it for free in

76
00:03:16,439 --> 00:03:17,611

77
00:03:17,631 --> 00:03:19,123
Claudius lost money.

78
00:03:19,143 --> 00:03:21,341

79
00:03:21,361 --> 00:03:24,021
Then, in early twenty twenty-six,

80
00:03:24,041 --> 00:03:29,651
Anthropic got so good at its job that it scared the rest of Wall Street.

81
00:03:30,955 --> 00:03:33,439
January twelfth, twenty twenty-six.

82
00:03:33,459 --> 00:03:36,691
Anthropic launches Claude Cowork, an AI that

83
00:03:36,711 --> 00:03:39,235
doesn't just chat, it does office work.

84
00:03:39,255 --> 00:03:43,261

85
00:03:43,281 --> 00:03:44,913

86
00:03:44,933 --> 00:03:46,805
If an AI can do the work,

87
00:03:46,825 --> 00:03:49,977

88
00:03:49,997 --> 00:03:51,417
In early February,

89
00:03:51,437 --> 00:03:56,349

90
00:03:56,369 --> 00:04:1,033
Thomson Reuters, the company behind Reuters, falls sixteen percent,

91
00:04:1,053 --> 00:04:2,595

92
00:04:2,615 --> 00:04:4,336
What did Anthropic release?

93
00:04:4,356 --> 00:04:5,234
Plugins.

94
00:04:5,254 --> 00:04:7,179
How many plugins?

95
00:04:7,199 --> 00:04:7,933
Eleven.

96
00:04:7,953 --> 00:04:12,093
That same month, investors put in thirty billion dollars,

97
00:04:12,113 --> 00:04:15,325

98
00:04:15,345 --> 00:04:17,197

99
00:04:17,217 --> 00:04:19,677
And Dario sits down for a long podcast

100
00:04:19,697 --> 00:04:22,157

101
00:04:22,177 --> 00:04:23,389
rented compute.

102
00:04:23,409 --> 00:04:24,437
We'll come back to it.

103
00:04:24,457 --> 00:04:26,229
Then the government turns.

104
00:04:26,249 --> 00:04:30,869
Anthropic had refused to let Claude be used for mass surveillance at home or for

105
00:04:30,889 --> 00:04:32,661
weapons that fire on their own.

106
00:04:32,681 --> 00:04:34,773
So on February twenty-seventh,

107
00:04:34,793 --> 00:04:38,720
Pete Hegseth's Pentagon labels it a supply chain risk.

108
00:04:38,740 --> 00:04:42,053
As of today, Anthropic is a supply chain risk.

109
00:04:42,073 --> 00:04:45,963
Isn't that label for companies from rival countries?

110
00:04:46,460 --> 00:04:47,335
Next question.

111
00:04:47,355 --> 00:04:48,687
He's right, by the way.

112
00:04:48,707 --> 00:04:51,407
Anthropic's own lawyers say the losses this

113
00:04:51,427 --> 00:04:53,327
year could run from hundreds of millions

114
00:04:53,347 --> 00:04:55,879
of dollars to multiple billions.

115
00:04:55,899 --> 00:04:58,831
For a company getting ready to ask the public for money,

116
00:04:58,851 --> 00:05:1,322
this is how the whole plan dies.

117
00:05:1,342 --> 00:05:2,219
It didn't.

118
00:05:2,239 --> 00:05:4,671
Because the government was never the money.

119
00:05:4,691 --> 00:05:7,490
It's less than two percent of Anthropic's sales.

120
00:05:7,510 --> 00:05:11,663
The Pentagon deal at the center of the fight was worth about two hundred million

121
00:05:11,683 --> 00:05:13,368
dollars over two years.

122
00:05:13,388 --> 00:05:16,583
These days, Anthropic sells that much in about a day.

123
00:05:16,603 --> 00:05:20,115
And the spring is the best stretch it has ever had.

124
00:05:20,135 --> 00:05:24,587
From April to June, sales hit eleven point six billion dollars,

125
00:05:24,607 --> 00:05:25,879
and for the first time,

126
00:05:25,899 --> 00:05:30,583
the business makes an operating profit: nine hundred and seventy-four million.

127
00:05:30,603 --> 00:05:33,863
Operating profit means what you make selling the thing,

128
00:05:33,883 --> 00:05:35,695
minus what it costs to make it.

129
00:05:35,715 --> 00:05:37,947
Claude finally paid for itself.

130
00:05:37,967 --> 00:05:42,699
In May, investors put in another sixty-five billion dollars,

131
00:05:42,719 --> 00:05:45,851
at a value of nine hundred and sixty-five billion.

132
00:05:45,871 --> 00:05:48,963
Remember that first round of a hundred and twenty-four million?

133
00:05:48,983 --> 00:05:52,237
This one is over five hundred times bigger.

134
00:05:52,257 --> 00:05:56,289
That's more than double February's price, in about three months.

135
00:05:56,309 --> 00:05:58,241
Which is fantastic news.

136
00:05:58,261 --> 00:06:3,751
And, as it turns out, the reason it lost eighty billion dollars.

137
00:06:5,085 --> 00:06:7,437
June first, twenty twenty-six.

138
00:06:7,457 --> 00:06:11,621
Anthropic sends its IPO paperwork to regulators, in secret.

139
00:06:11,641 --> 00:06:14,507
Eleven days later, somebody else goes first.

140
00:06:14,527 --> 00:06:18,079
SpaceX lists at a hundred and thirty-five dollars a share,

141
00:06:18,099 --> 00:06:20,631
worth one point seven seven trillion,

142
00:06:20,651 --> 00:06:24,023
with almost a third of the shares set aside for regular people.

143
00:06:24,043 --> 00:06:27,195
Day one, it closes at a hundred and sixty-one.

144
00:06:27,215 --> 00:06:29,827
Then it peaks at two hundred and eleven.

145
00:06:29,847 --> 00:06:32,831
By the middle of July, it's below where it started.

146
00:06:32,851 --> 00:06:35,195
By early August, a hundred and eight.

147
00:06:35,215 --> 00:06:38,507
In about six weeks, half the peak is gone.

148
00:06:38,527 --> 00:06:41,822
That's the chart Anthropic's bankers get to look at every morning.

149
00:06:41,842 --> 00:06:43,994
In October, the books leak.

150
00:06:44,014 --> 00:06:47,498
Then, on October twenty-sixth, the filing goes public.

151
00:06:47,518 --> 00:06:50,190
Its ticker will be ANT.

152
00:06:50,210 --> 00:06:54,634
Sales in the first half of the year: sixteen point three billion dollars,

153
00:06:54,654 --> 00:06:57,946
up from about one point two billion a year earlier.

154
00:06:57,966 --> 00:06:59,930
Loss: eighty point seven billion.

155
00:06:59,950 --> 00:07:4,323
The draft's list of things that could go wrong ran ninety-four pages.

156
00:07:4,343 --> 00:07:7,438
We're worth more than twice what we were in February.

157
00:07:7,458 --> 00:07:8,210
Correct.

158
00:07:8,230 --> 00:07:10,292
Congratulations.

159
00:07:10,326 --> 00:07:14,518
Then why does this say we lost seventy-two billion dollars?

160
00:07:14,538 --> 00:07:17,884
Because you're worth more than twice what you were in February.

161
00:07:17,904 --> 00:07:19,576
Remember the IOUs?

162
00:07:19,596 --> 00:07:20,376
Amazon,

163
00:07:20,396 --> 00:07:22,616
Google and other early backers gave

164
00:07:22,636 --> 00:07:25,908
Anthropic cash in exchange for shares later.

165
00:07:25,928 --> 00:07:27,300
Picture a lemonade stand.

166
00:07:27,320 --> 00:07:30,980
Your neighbor gives you a hundred dollars today for a slice of the stand,

167
00:07:31,000 --> 00:07:32,792
handed over down the road.

168
00:07:32,812 --> 00:07:36,204
Then your stand becomes the hottest stand in America.

169
00:07:36,224 --> 00:07:40,008
That slice is now worth a fortune, and you still owe it.

170
00:07:40,028 --> 00:07:44,404
The accounting rules say: the more your promise is worth, the more you owe.

171
00:07:44,424 --> 00:07:46,910
And that jump goes on the books as a loss.

172
00:07:46,930 --> 00:07:49,442
Out of the eighty point seven billion,

173
00:07:49,462 --> 00:07:52,634

174
00:07:52,654 --> 00:07:54,439
A charge on paper.

175
00:07:54,459 --> 00:07:57,035
So did any actual money leave?

176
00:07:57,055 --> 00:07:58,259
Not for that part.

177
00:07:58,279 --> 00:08:0,991
Look only at the business of selling Claude,

178
00:08:1,011 --> 00:08:4,963
and it lost about seven hundred million dollars in those six months.

179
00:08:4,983 --> 00:08:6,195
That's real money.

180
00:08:6,215 --> 00:08:8,947
It's also a long way from eighty billion.

181
00:08:8,967 --> 00:08:11,187
And over the first nine months of the year,

182
00:08:11,207 --> 00:08:15,987
the business itself brought in six point six billion dollars more than it cost to

183
00:08:16,007 --> 00:08:16,471

184
00:08:16,491 --> 00:08:17,743
Now flip it around.

185
00:08:17,763 --> 00:08:20,535
Amazon owns a pile of those IOUs.

186
00:08:20,555 --> 00:08:25,487
On its own books, it reported gains of more than sixty billion dollars from them.

187
00:08:25,507 --> 00:08:26,459
Same promise.

188
00:08:26,479 --> 00:08:28,271

189
00:08:28,291 --> 00:08:29,830

190
00:08:29,850 --> 00:08:31,262

191
00:08:31,282 --> 00:08:32,582
On November second,

192
00:08:32,602 --> 00:08:37,314

193
00:08:37,334 --> 00:08:38,066

00:08:41,898 --> 00:08:44,310

00:08:48,942 --> 00:08:49,482
Meanwhile,

More than it lost.

200
00:08:55,506 --> 00:08:56,588
Both numbers are true.

201
00:08:56,608 --> 00:08:59,148
So the scary number on the thumbnail is

202
00:08:59,168 --> 00:09:1,988
mostly a scoreboard of how fast Anthropic's

203
00:09:2,008 --> 00:09:2,760
value went up.

204
00:09:2,780 --> 00:09:3,623
Case closed?

205
00:09:3,643 --> 00:09:4,795
Not quite.

206
00:09:4,815 --> 00:09:8,187
Because buried in the same filing is a different number.

207
00:09:8,207 --> 00:09:10,857
And that one is real.

208
00:09:12,169 --> 00:09:15,301
Eight hundred and ninety-five billion dollars.

209
00:09:15,321 --> 00:09:19,473
That's how much Anthropic has signed up to pay for computers in the years ahead.

210
00:09:19,493 --> 00:09:22,557
Its sales so far this year: thirty-three billion.

211
00:09:22,577 --> 00:09:25,567
The bill is about twenty-seven times bigger.

212
00:09:25,587 --> 00:09:26,839
Here's who gets paid.

213
00:09:26,859 --> 00:09:29,663
Broadcom, about a hundred and sixty billion.

214
00:09:29,683 --> 00:09:31,415
Google, a hundred and twenty.

215
00:09:31,435 --> 00:09:33,607
Amazon, a hundred and ten.

216
00:09:33,627 --> 00:09:35,399
Microsoft, forty-five.

217
00:09:35,419 --> 00:09:39,451
And about a hundred and twenty billion to SpaceX's AI business.

218
00:09:39,471 --> 00:09:41,283
Yes, that SpaceX.

219
00:09:41,303 --> 00:09:46,554
The company whose IPO record Anthropic is chasing is also one of its landlords.

220
00:09:46,574 --> 00:09:48,354
Some of it can be cancelled,

221
00:09:48,374 --> 00:09:52,358
or depends on conditions: about two hundred and fourteen billion.

222
00:09:52,378 --> 00:09:55,550
But seventy billion is due in the next twelve months,

223
00:09:55,570 --> 00:09:59,163
and almost four hundred and fifty billion before twenty thirty-one.

224
00:09:59,183 --> 00:10:2,095
Why sign for so much, so far ahead?

225
00:10:2,115 --> 00:10:4,947
Because compute gets rented years in advance.

226
00:10:4,967 --> 00:10:7,859
Book too little, and you pay the last-minute price.

227
00:10:7,879 --> 00:10:9,931
That's exactly what happened this summer.

228
00:10:9,951 --> 00:10:15,843
From July to September, computers cost Anthropic nine point nine billion dollars,

229
00:10:15,863 --> 00:10:17,795
up seventy-seven percent.

230
00:10:17,815 --> 00:10:21,907
Five billion of that was expensive capacity grabbed at short notice.

231
00:10:21,927 --> 00:10:25,155
The business slipped back into a small operating loss.

232
00:10:25,175 --> 00:10:26,435
We need more computers.

233
00:10:26,455 --> 00:10:26,951
Today.

234
00:10:26,971 --> 00:10:28,999
Today costs more.

235
00:10:29,019 --> 00:10:30,605
How much have you got?

236
00:10:30,625 --> 00:10:33,529
About five billion dollars' worth.

237
00:10:33,549 --> 00:10:38,233
So that's one way to get it wrong: buy too little, and you pay through the nose.

238
00:10:38,253 --> 00:10:41,343
The other way is to buy too much.

239
00:10:42,683 --> 00:10:44,155
Which brings us to you.

240
00:10:44,175 --> 00:10:46,787
Here's how a company sells itself to the public.

241
00:10:46,807 --> 00:10:48,291
First, the filing.

242
00:10:48,311 --> 00:10:50,803
Then the roadshow: for about a week,

243
00:10:50,823 --> 00:10:54,095
bankers pitch the company to the biggest funds on Earth.

244
00:10:54,115 --> 00:10:57,959
The funds place orders: this many shares, at this price.

245
00:10:57,979 --> 00:10:59,759
The night before trading starts,

246
00:10:59,779 --> 00:11:3,191
the company and its banks pick the price that fills the book.

247
00:11:3,211 --> 00:11:7,618
Then the market opens, and the price does whatever it wants.

248
00:11:7,638 --> 00:11:9,069
How much did it lose?

249
00:11:9,089 --> 00:11:10,690
Which loss?

250
00:11:10,710 --> 00:11:11,850
The big one.

251
00:11:11,870 --> 00:11:14,166
Oh, that one's good news.

252
00:11:14,186 --> 00:11:16,269
Then we'll pay the low end.

253
00:11:16,289 --> 00:11:20,821
Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley lead it, with twenty-two banks in all.

254
00:11:20,841 --> 00:11:25,125
One more thing to know: Anthropic only gets the money from new shares.

255
00:11:25,145 --> 00:11:29,217
When early holders sell their shares in the deal, that money goes to them.

256
00:11:29,237 --> 00:11:32,249
And most insiders can't sell for six months anyway.

257
00:11:32,269 --> 00:11:34,545
The founders, for up to about a year.

258
00:11:34,565 --> 00:11:37,177
Regular people get a real seat this time.

259
00:11:37,197 --> 00:11:41,901
The filing names six brokers, from Schwab and Fidelity to Robinhood.

260
00:11:41,921 --> 00:11:45,933
Reports say the public could get fifteen to twenty percent of the shares.

261
00:11:45,953 --> 00:11:50,013
And in September, Anthropic split every share into ten,

262
00:11:50,033 --> 00:11:51,530
before the public could buy one.

263
00:11:51,550 --> 00:11:55,422
The price talk is one and a half to two trillion dollars.

264
00:11:55,442 --> 00:11:57,514
The big funds are pushing for the low end.

265
00:11:57,534 --> 00:11:58,346
Even there,

266
00:11:58,366 --> 00:12:3,106
buyers pay about forty-three dollars for every dollar of sales Anthropic made over

267
00:12:3,126 --> 00:12:4,558
the past twelve months.

268
00:12:4,578 --> 00:12:6,633
At two trillion, fifty-seven.

269
00:12:6,653 --> 00:12:9,753
Jay Ritter, the professor Wall Street calls Mr.

270
00:12:9,773 --> 00:12:11,605
IPO, has counted.

271
00:12:11,625 --> 00:12:16,525
Out of four thousand one hundred and ten American IPOs from nineteen eighty to

272
00:12:16,545 --> 00:12:21,209
twenty twenty-four, only fourteen priced at forty times sales or more.

273
00:12:21,229 --> 00:12:24,745
On average, they did fifteen percent worse than the market.

274
00:12:24,765 --> 00:12:28,417
Aswath Damodaran, who values companies for a living,

275
00:12:28,437 --> 00:12:30,417
called the latest quarter "the most

276
00:12:30,437 --> 00:12:33,289
telegraphed third quarter number of all time."

277
00:12:33,309 --> 00:12:37,381
He puts Anthropic at about one point four seven five trillion.

278
00:12:37,401 --> 00:12:38,850
Just under the low end.

279
00:12:38,870 --> 00:12:42,062
Now, back to February, and that podcast.

280
00:12:42,082 --> 00:12:46,454
Dario was talking about the danger of a lab buying compute too early,

281
00:12:46,474 --> 00:12:48,106
years ahead of the customers.

282
00:12:48,126 --> 00:12:49,411
He didn't soften it.

283
00:12:49,431 --> 00:12:52,243
If I'm just off by a year in that rate of growth,

284
00:12:52,263 --> 00:12:55,975
or if the growth rate is five x a year instead of ten x a year,

285
00:12:55,995 --> 00:12:57,073
then you go bankrupt.

286
00:12:57,093 --> 00:12:59,605
That's not someone betting against the stock.

287
00:12:59,625 --> 00:13:4,289
That's the CEO, describing the trap his whole industry is standing in.

288
00:13:4,309 --> 00:13:6,209
Anthropic has signed eight hundred and

289
00:13:6,229 --> 00:13:8,929
ninety-five billion dollars of bills on the

290
00:13:8,949 --> 00:13:11,141
bet that growth shows up on schedule.

291
00:13:11,161 --> 00:13:13,527
Now it's asking the public to buy in.

292
00:13:13,547 --> 00:13:14,819
Here's where it stands.

293
00:13:14,839 --> 00:13:17,871
The roadshow can start as early as November tenth,

294
00:13:17,891 --> 00:13:21,223
with trading planned for mid-November, the week of the sixteenth.

295
00:13:21,243 --> 00:13:26,007
The Pentagon fight stands at a split: a judge threw out one label in August,

296
00:13:26,027 --> 00:13:28,699
and an appeals court kept the other in September.

297
00:13:28,719 --> 00:13:33,483
SpaceX, the record holder, is trading right back around its IPO price.

298
00:13:33,503 --> 00:13:35,003
And whatever the price,

299
00:13:35,023 --> 00:13:39,055
the seven co-founders keep control through one special share.

300
00:13:39,075 --> 00:13:42,439
One share, with fifty point one percent of the vote.

301
00:13:42,459 --> 00:13:45,433
They've also pledged eighty percent of their stake to charity.

302
00:13:45,453 --> 00:13:48,705
Eighty billion dollars sounds like the end of a company.

303
00:13:48,725 --> 00:13:52,057
Here, it's mostly the receipt for becoming more valuable.

304
00:13:52,077 --> 00:13:56,249
The number that decides this story is the one nobody puts on a thumbnail.

305
00:13:56,269 --> 00:14:0,933
Eight hundred and ninety-five billion dollars of computers, already booked.

306
00:14:0,953 --> 00:14:3,074
Now the customers have to show up on time.

307
00:14:3,094 --> 00:14:3,714
As Mr.

308
00:14:3,734 --> 00:14:8,016
IPO put it, "a lot of things have to go right."

Why Nvidia is in trouble without Jensen Huang, who resigned as CEO on 12 November 2026, days before the company's earnings report on Tuesday 17 November.

Jensen Huang ran Nvidia for 33 years with sixty people reporting straight to him and no number two. He made the bets a finance chief would have refused, like paying for CUDA for years while it earned almost nothing. Now his finance chief, Colette Kress, is interim CEO, and when HP and Intel handed the company to the CFO, both fell behind.

Can Nvidia survive without him?

1
00:00:0,300 --> 00:00:1,352
This is Jensen.

2
00:00:1,372 --> 00:00:4,013
And Jensen has a huge problem.

3
00:00:4,033 --> 00:00:6,599
For thirty-three years, he built one company.

4
00:00:6,619 --> 00:00:8,990
It almost went broke, and he saved it.

5
00:00:9,010 --> 00:00:12,542
He bet a huge share of his profits on software nobody wanted,

6
00:00:12,562 --> 00:00:14,539
and waited ten years to be right.

7
00:00:14,559 --> 00:00:18,812
He turned a video game chip maker into the most valuable company on Earth.

8
00:00:18,832 --> 00:00:20,464
Thirty-three years.

9
00:00:20,484 --> 00:00:24,322
And this week he lost it, because he couldn't keep his pants zipped.

10
00:00:24,342 --> 00:00:26,079
We accept your resignation.

11
00:00:26,099 --> 00:00:27,547
Can I keep the jacket?

12
00:00:27,567 --> 00:00:28,102
No.

13
00:00:28,122 --> 00:00:29,994
But that's Jensen's problem.

14
00:00:30,014 --> 00:00:31,291
Here's Nvidia's.

15
00:00:31,311 --> 00:00:33,343
Nobody thought he would actually go.

16
00:00:33,363 --> 00:00:37,201
Two days before he quit, the betting markets gave it eighteen percent.

17
00:00:37,221 --> 00:00:39,973
Because nobody could picture Nvidia without him.

18
00:00:39,993 --> 00:00:42,085
Nvidia never had a number two.

19
00:00:42,105 --> 00:00:44,897
Sixty people reported straight to one man.

20
00:00:44,917 --> 00:00:45,709
No backup.

21
00:00:45,729 --> 00:00:46,548
No plan B.

22
00:00:46,568 --> 00:00:48,660
There has to be somebody else.

23
00:00:48,680 --> 00:00:50,034
The guy in the leather jacket.

24
00:00:50,054 --> 00:00:50,991
That's Jensen.

25
00:00:51,011 --> 00:00:53,727
The other guy in the leather jacket?

26
00:00:53,747 --> 00:00:55,959
Wall Street has even put a price on it.

27
00:00:55,979 --> 00:00:58,051
One analyst says Nvidia is worth three

28
00:00:58,071 --> 00:01:0,051
hundred dollars a share with Jensen in that

29
00:01:0,071 --> 00:01:0,703
jacket.

30
00:01:0,723 --> 00:01:2,815
And two hundred twenty-five with it empty.

31
00:01:2,835 --> 00:01:5,637
That gap is almost two trillion dollars.

32
00:01:5,657 --> 00:01:8,169
Right now, the finance chief is holding it.

33
00:01:8,189 --> 00:01:10,301
The President wants to hand it to Tim Cook.

34
00:01:10,321 --> 00:01:14,748
And on Tuesday, Nvidia reports its numbers without him for the first time ever.

35
00:01:14,768 --> 00:01:18,140
So how does a man throw away thirty-three years of work?

36
00:01:18,160 --> 00:01:19,692
We've told that story already.

37
00:01:19,712 --> 00:01:22,184
The big question is the one he left behind.

38
00:01:22,204 --> 00:01:25,054
Can Nvidia survive without him?

39
00:01:28,452 --> 00:01:30,284
April nineteen ninety-three.

40
00:01:30,304 --> 00:01:34,336
Jensen Huang and two other engineers start a graphics chip company.

41
00:01:34,356 --> 00:01:35,566
They call it Nvidia.

42
00:01:35,586 --> 00:01:36,243
Jensen.

43
00:01:36,263 --> 00:01:39,515
Microsoft just set the rules for PC games.

44
00:01:39,535 --> 00:01:41,243
Everything's triangles.

45
00:01:41,263 --> 00:01:43,765
Our chip does curves.

46
00:01:43,785 --> 00:01:44,895
Only curves.

47
00:01:44,915 --> 00:01:49,307
Nvidia has cut a beautiful key for a lock that just got changed.

48
00:01:49,327 --> 00:01:53,383
Worse, its biggest customer, Sega, is paying for the next chip,

49
00:01:53,403 --> 00:01:55,175
built the same wrong way.

50
00:01:55,195 --> 00:01:57,179
So Jensen flies to Japan.

51
00:01:57,199 --> 00:01:58,871
Our chip is a dead end.

52
00:01:58,891 --> 00:02:0,163
Cancel our contract.

53
00:02:0,183 --> 00:02:1,432
Hire someone else.

54
00:02:1,452 --> 00:02:3,747
You flew here to fire yourself?

55
00:02:3,767 --> 00:02:4,379
Yes.

56
00:02:4,399 --> 00:02:7,251
And keep the money you still owe us inside Nvidia.

57
00:02:7,271 --> 00:02:8,205
As an investment.

58
00:02:8,225 --> 00:02:10,345
In the company whose chip doesn't work.

59
00:02:10,365 --> 00:02:11,763
You'll probably lose it.

60
00:02:11,783 --> 00:02:13,250
Sega said yes.

61
00:02:13,270 --> 00:02:16,739
Five million dollars, and it kept Nvidia alive.

62
00:02:16,759 --> 00:02:17,471
The reason?

63
00:02:17,491 --> 00:02:20,062
Sega's boss simply believed in him.

64
00:02:20,082 --> 00:02:21,583
How long have we got?

65
00:02:21,603 --> 00:02:22,515
Thirty days.

66
00:02:22,535 --> 00:02:23,397
Same as always.

67
00:02:23,417 --> 00:02:27,241
That was the company's motto: thirty days from going out of business.

68
00:02:27,261 --> 00:02:31,945
In nineteen ninety-seven, its next chip sold about a million in four months,

69
00:02:31,965 --> 00:02:35,741
and within a few years, Nvidia was the king of gaming chips.

70
00:02:35,761 --> 00:02:37,653
Then, in two thousand six,

71
00:02:37,673 --> 00:02:41,865
Jensen spent a big piece of the money on something gamers would never see.

72
00:02:41,885 --> 00:02:43,146
He called it CUDA.

73
00:02:43,166 --> 00:02:46,233
A graphics chip does thousands of tiny sums at once.

74
00:02:46,253 --> 00:02:48,516
Scientists could use that for anything.

75
00:02:48,536 --> 00:02:49,652
Who pays for it?

76
00:02:49,672 --> 00:02:50,424
Nobody.

77
00:02:50,444 --> 00:02:50,910
Yet.

78
00:02:50,930 --> 00:02:54,042
It cost Nvidia a huge share of its profits,

79
00:02:54,062 --> 00:02:56,624
and for years it earned almost nothing.

80
00:02:56,644 --> 00:02:57,916
Three years.

81
00:02:57,936 --> 00:02:59,008
Still flat.

82
00:02:59,028 --> 00:03:0,695
It's eating our margins.

83
00:03:0,715 --> 00:03:1,528
It's early.

84
00:03:1,548 --> 00:03:4,063
I can't put "early" in a forecast.

85
00:03:4,083 --> 00:03:5,875
Then leave it out of the forecast.

86
00:03:5,895 --> 00:03:6,810
Keep it in the company.

87
00:03:6,830 --> 00:03:11,940
In twenty twelve, a team in Toronto won an image-recognition contest by a mile,

88
00:03:11,960 --> 00:03:15,272
with a program trained on two Nvidia gaming cards.

89
00:03:15,292 --> 00:03:17,736
Every AI lab on Earth noticed.

90
00:03:17,756 --> 00:03:19,888
CUDA took a decade to pay off.

91
00:03:19,908 --> 00:03:24,404
Today, nine of every ten graphics chips that run AI are Nvidia's.

92
00:03:24,424 --> 00:03:25,776
And that finance chief?

93
00:03:25,796 --> 00:03:26,548
He was right.

94
00:03:26,568 --> 00:03:30,332
Every year CUDA lost money, cutting it was the sensible call.

95
00:03:30,352 --> 00:03:35,696
Even the investors who think Nvidia will be fine give Jensen's pipeline two years.

96
00:03:35,716 --> 00:03:37,548
So who signs year three?

97
00:03:37,568 --> 00:03:41,970
As of this week, Nvidia's boss is its finance chief.

98
00:03:43,259 --> 00:03:44,551
Back to that test.

99
00:03:44,571 --> 00:03:48,029
Name one Nvidia executive who isn't Jensen Huang.

100
00:03:48,049 --> 00:03:49,041
You can't.

101
00:03:49,061 --> 00:03:50,293
That was on purpose.

102
00:03:50,313 --> 00:03:54,916
For years, Jensen was Nvidia's only face, inside and out.

103
00:03:54,936 --> 00:03:57,780
Most big companies are built like an office tower.

104
00:03:57,800 --> 00:04:0,328
Nvidia was built like a bicycle wheel.

105
00:04:0,348 --> 00:04:2,920
Sixty people reported straight to Jensen.

106
00:04:2,940 --> 00:04:4,792
No chief operating officer.

107
00:04:4,812 --> 00:04:5,902
No one-on-ones.

108
00:04:5,922 --> 00:04:9,077
"I don't have one-on-ones with them because it's impossible."

109
00:04:9,097 --> 00:04:11,718
He even reviewed every employee's pay.

110
00:04:11,738 --> 00:04:12,946
Who needs a decision?

111
00:04:12,966 --> 00:04:13,544
Me.

112
00:04:13,564 --> 00:04:14,104
Yes.

113
00:04:14,124 --> 00:04:14,664
Yes.

114
00:04:14,684 --> 00:04:15,096
No.

115
00:04:15,116 --> 00:04:15,736
Yes.

116
00:04:15,756 --> 00:04:16,165
Next.

117
00:04:16,185 --> 00:04:18,037
It made Nvidia fast.

118
00:04:18,057 --> 00:04:19,609
In Jensen's own words,

119
00:04:19,629 --> 00:04:24,001
"My management style is what made it possible for the company to grow." It also

120
00:04:24,021 --> 00:04:25,033
meant this.

121
00:04:25,053 --> 00:04:26,834
So who's number two?

122
00:04:26,854 --> 00:04:27,866
There isn't one.

123
00:04:27,886 --> 00:04:29,532
No succession plan either.

124
00:04:29,552 --> 00:04:31,504
So what was the hub holding?

125
00:04:31,524 --> 00:04:32,914
First, the customers.

126
00:04:32,934 --> 00:04:34,812
Who buys all these chips?

127
00:04:34,832 --> 00:04:36,224
Three direct buyers.

128
00:04:36,244 --> 00:04:39,475
About forty-four cents of every dollar, this year so far.

129
00:04:39,495 --> 00:04:40,971
And who did they deal with?

130
00:04:40,991 --> 00:04:41,579
Guess.

131
00:04:41,599 --> 00:04:46,515
One investor, Thomas Ferguson, said this: "As a student of economic history,

132
00:04:46,535 --> 00:04:51,179
I don't know if there's ever been such a key man holding so much of this industry

133
00:04:51,199 --> 00:04:51,499
up."

134
00:04:51,519 --> 00:04:53,906
And that industry includes your money.

135
00:04:53,926 --> 00:04:55,778
I don't own Nvidia.

136
00:04:55,798 --> 00:04:58,681
Got an S&P five hundred fund in there?

137
00:04:58,701 --> 00:04:59,199
Yes.

138
00:04:59,219 --> 00:05:0,594
Then you own Nvidia.

139
00:05:0,614 --> 00:05:3,968
Put ten thousand dollars in an S&P five hundred fund,

140
00:05:3,988 --> 00:05:6,580
and six or seven hundred of it is Nvidia.

141
00:05:6,600 --> 00:05:11,104
One of the biggest bets in your whole retirement is riding on one company.

142
00:05:11,124 --> 00:05:13,788
And that company was riding on one man.

143
00:05:13,808 --> 00:05:15,628
I never picked this guy.
